title: As-Sami' and al-Basir
hookLine: the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, who hears whispers and sees the ant

cards: A woman in Medina has a bad problem at home. Her husband has said an old Arabian oath that leaves her neither married nor free. She comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and she argues.
She pleads. She complains, out loud, to God. His wife Aisha is in the same room, and she said later that she could not even hear all of what the woman was saying.
It was that quiet. Then verses came down that begin: God has heard the words of the woman who argued with you about her husband. The person in the room missed some of it.
The one she was really talking to missed none of it.

teach.b: As-Sami': the All-Hearing, from sam', hearing. Al-Basir: the All-Seeing, from basar, sight. In the Qur'an they often come as a pair at the end of a verse, like two notes of one chord.
One verse, in Pickthall's old translation: "Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer."
First it says nothing is like him. Then it uses two words people use about themselves. Many Muslim scholars read it as a guard rail: God hears and sees, truly, but not with ears and eyes like ours.
Human hearing gets tired; His doesn't. Human sight needs light; His doesn't. A saying often repeated in Muslim teaching has God seeing a black ant on a black stone on a moonless night.
A picture, not a verse, but it makes the point: nothing is too small or too dark. And the pair isn't only about being watched.

teach.h: I AM WITH YOU, HEARING AND SEEING.
teach.b: When Musa and Harun, Moses and Aaron, are sent to face Pharaoh, they're afraid, and God tells them not to fear: "Lo! I am with you twain, Hearing and Seeing." That's comfort, not surveillance.
The woman in Medina had no lawyer, no power, no loud voice, and a complaint so quiet the person in the room missed some of it.
The chapter she's remembered in is named for her: al-Mujadilah, the woman who argues. The Prophet taught that when people call on God, they're not calling someone deaf or far away.

how: Muslims call on God as as-Sami' and al-Basir in private du'a, often quietly or silently, and many say after rising from bowing in prayer that God hears the one who praises him.

o: the one who listens to the prophets alone
the one who hears everything, even a whisper
the one who hears only the loudest voice

games.q: what's inside the names — tap the pairs.
p: I am with you, hearing and seeing

s: Aisha, in the same room, couldn't hear all the woman said
yet the verses began: God has heard her.
the black ant on the black stone is a verse of the Qur'an
it's a saying often repeated in Muslim teaching, a picture of the point, not a verse.
as-Sami' and al-Basir often come as a pair in the Qur'an
at the ends of verses, like two notes of one chord.

games.q: you're the woman in Medina. your husband's oath has left you stuck. nobody powerful is on your side. what do you do?
o: say nothing and put up with it.
bring your case to the Prophet and complain to God.
games.why: she argued and complained to God, so quietly Aisha missed some of it, and a whole surah opens with God has heard her.

practice: Let the room go quiet and find the loudest sound, then a quieter one under it, then the quietest you can catch: a fridge, a breath, a bird far off.

Open your eyes, find the smallest thing in view, a crumb, a thread, a speck of light, and hold the faintest sound and the smallest sight together. If you pray, you can call on God as as-Sami', al-Basir.

wordCard.voice: As-Sami', the All-Hearing: one of the two names, paired with al-Basir, the All-Seeing, that travel together through the Qur'an.

orig.note: Arabic: the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing. from sam' (hearing) and basar (sight).

carryVoice: Your line: heard, seen. Even where no one seems to notice: a meeting, a group chat, a kitchen. Back tomorrow.

sources.q: Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer.
Lo! I am with you twain, Hearing and Seeing.

sources.ref: Qur'an 58:1 (God has heard the woman who disputed with you about her husband)
Aisha's report that she could not hear all of Khawlah's words (Sunan Ibn Majah 188; Sunan an-Nasa'i 3460; cited by al-Bukhari in Kitab at-Tawhid)
hadith: you are not calling one who is deaf or absent (Sahih al-Bukhari 2992)
